title: Writing technical blog posts
summary: Turn your projects into clear technical blog posts that show your thinking and help you get noticed by employers.
objectives: Understand why technical writing boosts your AI job search
Choose a focused topic and a single takeaway for a post
Structure a post: hook, problem, solution, results, lessons
Write reproducible code blocks readers can actually run
Add diagrams, results, and honest caveats to build trust
Publish on a free platform and share it the right way

quiz.q: What is the main career benefit of blogging for an aspiring AI engineer?
options: It shows your thinking and creates a public portfolio
quiz.why: A blog demonstrates how you reason and communicate — recruiters and engineers can see your work, which a CV alone cannot show.

quiz.q: What should every post have exactly one of?
quiz.why: Focusing each post on one main idea keeps it readable and memorable; readers should know what they learned in one sentence.

quiz.q: Why should code blocks in a post be runnable and self-contained?
quiz.answer: So readers can copy, paste, and reproduce your results without guessing missing imports or setup — reproducibility builds trust.
quiz.why: Broken or partial snippets frustrate readers and make you look careless; complete examples prove the post actually works.

quiz.q: Where should API keys appear in any code you publish?
options: In an environment variable, never in the text
quiz.why: Never paste secrets. Read them from environment variables like ANTHROPIC_API_KEY so you don't leak credentials to the public.

quiz.q: Name one good free platform for publishing a technical blog post.
quiz.answer: Dev.to, Hashnode, Medium, or GitHub Pages are all common free choices.
quiz.why: These give you a public URL, a built-in audience, and simple Markdown editing without managing servers.

quiz.q: What makes a post more trustworthy and honest?
options: Including caveats, limitations, and failed attempts
quiz.why: Sharing limitations and what didn't work signals real engineering maturity and helps readers avoid the same pitfalls.

body_markdown:
## Why blog at all?

You've built projects this course — a model, an A P I, a deployed app. A **technical blog post** turns that hidden work into something recruiters, engineers, and your future self can read. It shows not just *what* you built but *how you think*, which a CV alone never reveals.

Writing also sharpens your own understanding. If you can explain a confusion matrix clearly to a stranger, you truly understand it.

## Pick one idea

A strong post has **one takeaway**. Not "everything I learned about machine learning" — instead "how I cut my model's false positives in half." Narrow beats broad. Write the single sentence a reader should remember *before* you write anything else.

## A reliable structure

Most good technical posts follow the same shape:

1. **Hook** — a relatable problem in two sentences.
2. **Context** — what you were building and why.
3. **Solution** — the key steps, with code.
4. **Results** — numbers, screenshots, before/after.
5. **Lessons** — what you'd do differently.

## Make code reproducible

Readers will copy your code. Make it **complete**: real imports, no hidden setup, secrets in environment variables. Show a small, runnable example rather than your whole repo.

```python
import os
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from env

msg = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Summarise this post in one sentence."}],
)
print(msg.content[0].text)
```

Keep your key out of the text. Set it once in your shell:

```bash
export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="your-key-here"
python summarise.py
```

## Publish and share

Use a free platform — **Dev.to**, **Hashnode**, **Medium**, or **GitHub Pages**. Write in Markdown, add a clear title, and pick honest tags. Then share the link where engineers gather: LinkedIn, relevant Discord or Slack groups, and your network. One good post, shared well, beats ten posts no one reads.

## Your task

Pick one project from this course and **write a 600-word post** with one takeaway, one runnable code block, and one honest lesson. Publish it and share the U R L.

slides.narration: Welcome to Month Five, where we polish your work, deploy it, and go public. In this lesson we'll cover something that quietly transforms a job search: writing technical blog posts. By the end you'll know how to turn a project into a clear, reproducible post that shows employers how you think.

slides.title: Why blog at all?
bullets: Turns hidden project work into something readable.
Shows how you think, not just what you built.
A CV lists; a blog demonstrates.
slides.narration: So why should you blog? You've built real things this course, but that work is invisible until you write about it. A blog post shows recruiters and engineers how you reason through a problem, which a CV can never do. And here's a bonus: explaining something clearly forces you to truly understand it yourself.

slides.title: Pick one idea
bullets: Each post has exactly one takeaway.
slides.narration: The most common mistake is trying to say everything at once. A strong post has one takeaway. Not everything I learned about machine learning, but instead, how I cut my model's false positives in half. Before you write a single paragraph, write the one sentence you want the reader to remember.

slides.title: A reliable structure
bullets: Context: what you built and why.
Solution: the key steps and code.
slides.narration: Good technical posts share a simple shape. Start with a hook, a relatable problem in two sentences. Give context on what you were building. Then the solution with code, the results with real numbers, and finally the lessons you'd apply next time. This structure carries the reader from confusion to clarity.

slides.title: Make code reproducible
bullets: Include real imports, no hidden setup.
Keep secrets out of the text.
slides.code:
import os
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()
msg = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-4-6",
    max_tokens=1024,
    messages=[{"role": "user",
               "content": "Hi"}])
slides.narration: Readers will copy and paste your code, so make it complete. Include the real imports and no hidden setup. Here we create an Anthropic client and send one message to Claude using the messages API. Notice we don't paste a key anywhere, the client reads it from the environment. Show a small example, not your whole repository.

slides.title: Never leak secrets
bullets: Read with os.environ or the S D K.
Never paste a key into a snippet.
slides.narration: A quick but vital warning: never publish a secret. Keep your A P I keys in environment variables, like ANTHROPIC underscore A P I underscore KEY, and let the library read them. Don't paste a key into a code block, and double-check your screenshots too. A leaked key in a public post can cost you real money.

slides.title: Show real results
slides.narration: Results are what make a post convincing. Show numbers, a before and after, or a small chart. A single clear diagram often replaces three paragraphs of explanation. Screenshots prove your thing actually ran. Be specific: cut latency from two seconds to four hundred milliseconds is far stronger than made it faster.

slides.title: Be honest
bullets: It helps readers avoid your pitfalls.
slides.narration: The best technical writers are honest. Share what didn't work, the dead ends, and the limitations of your approach. This feels risky, but it's the opposite. Showing your failed attempts signals real engineering maturity, builds trust, and genuinely helps readers avoid the same traps you fell into.

slides.title: Publish and share
bullets: Or GitHub Pages from a repo.
slides.narration: Now publish. Use a free platform like Dev dot to, Hashnode, Medium, or GitHub Pages. You'll write in Markdown, which you already know. Then share the U R L where engineers actually gather: LinkedIn, relevant Discord or Slack groups, and your own network. One good post, shared well, beats ten posts nobody sees.
